lesson.title: Splitting Down the Middle: Disruptive Selection
lesson.summary: Disruptive selection favors both extremes of a trait's distribution over the intermediate middle, which can split a population's phenotype distribution into two distinct peaks and, in some cases, set the stage for the population to divide into two species.
lesson.body:
Disruptive selection, sometimes called diversifying selection, is the pattern in which individuals at both extremes of a trait's distribution have higher relative fitness than individuals near the middle. It is, in a sense, the opposite of stabilizing selection: instead of trimming both tails and favoring the average, disruptive selection favors both tails and selects against the average. Where stabilizing selection narrows a population's variation and directional selection shifts its average, disruptive selection can pull a single, unimodal distribution apart into two separate peaks, one clustered around each favored extreme, with fewer and fewer individuals occupying the middle ground as generations pass.

A well studied example comes from a species of African finch whose diet includes seeds from two different sedge plants, one with a soft seed coat and one with a much harder one. Birds with small, narrow bills are efficient at cracking the soft seeds but struggle with the hard ones. Birds with large, deep bills are efficient at cracking the hard seeds but are comparatively less efficient at handling the soft ones. Birds with intermediate bill sizes turn out to be mediocre at cracking either seed type, well suited to neither food source. Researchers studying wild populations of this finch found a bill size distribution with two distinct peaks, a cluster of small billed birds and a cluster of large billed birds, with comparatively few birds in between, exactly the pattern disruptive selection predicts when two distinct resources are both being exploited and an intermediate strategy is competitively inferior to either specialization.

Disruptive selection is unusual among the three patterns in that it can increase, rather than decrease, the variation present in a population, at least in the sense of producing two well separated phenotype clusters instead of one central one. On its own, disruptive selection does not create two species. The small billed and large billed finches described above are still one interbreeding population, and their offspring, wherever bill size falls, remain part of the same gene pool. But if something additionally reduces interbreeding between the two phenotype clusters, individuals preferentially mating with others of a similar bill size, for instance, disruptive selection becomes one of the plausible starting points for a single population diverging into two, a connection worth keeping in mind heading into the discussion of species and speciation that follows.
